opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was more mixed than I expected, and I think that's healthy. Some people were really excited. They were glad to see a lab commit real resources to alignment and say publicly that we don't yet know how to steer and control systems that might end up much smarter than us. A lot of researchers reached out wanting to get involved, which was encouraging, because what this field needs most is more talented people working on the problem.

There was also a lot of skepticism, from a few directions. Some people think the whole framing is premature: why worry about superintelligence when current systems still make basic mistakes? Others, closer to the alignment community, worried that our plan leans too heavily on using AI systems to help with alignment research itself. Their concern is that this is circular, or that we'd be trusting systems we can't yet verify.

I take that second critique seriously. It's a bet, and we should be upfront about that. My view is that alignment research will have to scale alongside capabilities, and that's hard to do with human effort alone. So the question is whether we can build systems that are narrow and trustworthy enough to speed up the work, and whether we can check their outputs. Evaluation is generally easier than generation, and that asymmetry is a big part of why I'm optimistic.

What I'd most like is for the disagreement to turn into concrete research. If someone thinks our approach fails, the most useful thing is to say exactly where and why, ideally in a way we can test empirically. That's how we make progress, rather than just trading intuitions.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I thought the reaction was quite a bit more positive than I expected. I was bracing for a lot more pushback, and instead there was a lot of genuine engagement with the actual substance of what we were proposing.

I think part of what's going on is that the field has shifted. A few years ago, if you'd put out something saying "we're going to try to solve alignment for superhuman systems, and we think a big part of the answer is using AI to help us do alignment research," a lot of people would have dismissed that as speculative or science fiction. But now the systems are good enough that people can see the trajectory. It's much harder to argue that these problems are far off, because you can just look at what the models can do today and extrapolate a little bit.

There was criticism, of course, and I think some of it was fair. One line of criticism is basically: isn't it circular to use AI systems you don't trust to help you build AI systems you can trust? And I think that's a real question we have to take seriously. My answer is that evaluation is often easier than generation. If a model produces an alignment research result, we can scrutinize it, we can replicate it, we can check the reasoning. We don't need to blindly trust the model, we need to be able to evaluate its outputs, and that's a much lower bar. But people are right to push on exactly where that argument breaks down.

The other thing I'd say is that a lot of the skepticism was less about the technical approach and more about the institutional question. Can a lab actually prioritize this? Will it get the resources it needs when there's commercial pressure pulling in other directions? And I think those are legitimate concerns. I don't think I can resolve them by making arguments on a podcast. The only way to answer them is to actually do the work and show results.

So overall I'd say: more support than I expected, criticism that was mostly thoughtful, and a lot of people who are now more interested in working on these problems. That last part is probably the thing I care about most.

astra-6.text:
I think the reaction reflects a real disagreement about how seriously to take the possibility of very capable AI systems, and how soon we need to prepare for them. If you think that’s a distant prospect, then a research agenda focused on aligning those systems can seem premature. If you think it could happen relatively soon, it seems important to start now.

There’s also reasonable skepticism about whether the approaches we’re proposing will work. I share that uncertainty. Announcing a research direction isn’t the same as having solved the problem. What I’d like is for us to turn those disagreements into concrete research questions: where do these methods fail, what can we test today, and what evidence would give us more confidence?

sol-6.1.text:
I think the reaction reflects a real disagreement about how hard alignment is going to be, and what we should be working on now. Some people think that keeping systems aligned will be a fairly natural extension of making them useful. Others think that once systems become much more capable than we are, our current methods could break down quite badly.

My view is that we don’t yet have enough evidence to be confident that this will be easy. And because the consequences of getting it wrong could be so significant, it makes sense to put serious effort into it now. You don’t have to agree with every prediction about future AI to think that understanding how to reliably supervise these systems is an important research problem.
